messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Film Director
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Distraction: I distract myself with something else
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arthur was a man accustomed to control. As a film director for over two decades, his job was to command chaos—to orchestrate light, sound, and performance into a coherent vision. That sense of command shattered six months ago during a night shoot in a repurposed industrial warehouse. He remembers it not as a story, but as a sequence of stark, silent images: the slow buckle of a steel support beam under the lighting rig, the cloud of dust blooming towards the ceiling, the look of surprise on his cinematographer’s face just before the world went black. He can’t seem to put the sequence into words, but the pictures are perfectly, terribly clear. The crushing weight and the sudden, absolute darkness were followed by a sound he can never forget—the deafening shriek of twisting metal.

These flashes of memory, vivid and intrusive, are not just frightening; for Arthur, they have become evidence of his own failure. He sees the image of himself, frozen for a split second before the collapse, and has come to believe he is fundamentally inadequate, a leader who failed to protect his crew. The clarity of these visual fragments serves as a constant reminder of his perceived helplessness, cementing a deep conviction that his reactions prove he is a lousy coper. This belief that he is no longer the capable man he once was makes the world feel impossibly dangerous. If he couldn't handle that moment, he feels certain he cannot handle the future, a fear that keeps his body in a constant state of high alert, scanning every room and bracing for the next catastrophe. His nervous system now seems wired directly to the memory; any sudden, loud sound doesn’t just startle him, it brings the image of falling steel rushing back, his heart pounding as if it’s happening all over again.

This pervasive sense of threat has made his own work environment, once a place of creation, a minefield of triggers. The sudden shout of "Action!", the controlled bang of a prop gun, the deep shadows of a soundstage—all send a jolt of panic through him. To manage this relentless, exhausting state of being superalert, Arthur has begun to fundamentally alter how he lives and works. He avoids circumstances that remind him of the event, most notably darkness. He insists on keeping lights on in every room of the house he shares with his partner and has started turning down projects that require extensive night shoots or location work in dark, enclosed spaces. This retreat is fueled by the shame of who he has become; he feels like an imposter, a man unrecognisable to himself, and his avoidance is a way to hide this new, fragile identity from his colleagues and from himself.

This strategy of avoidance, however, has only tightened the trap. By refusing to enter dark screening rooms or work on loud sets, the memories of the accident have remained frozen and unprocessed. The darkness he so carefully avoids has become inextricably linked with the crushing weight of the collapsed rig, making the visual fragments even more potent and terrifying when they inevitably break through. Each time he makes an excuse to his agent or cancels a meeting, the belief that he is a "lousy coper" intensifies. His shrinking world is, to him, daily proof that the competent, confident director is gone. He also finds himself lost in thought, trying to make sense of it all, constantly asking himself why the event happened to him, a question with no satisfying answer. When this mental churning becomes too much, he distracts himself for hours with old films, a temporary reprieve that only makes the ambient sounds of the city—a car backfiring, a distant siren—feel more jarring and threatening when they finally cut through the quiet.

Arthur finally sought therapy after a humiliating experience last week. During a pre-production meeting in a state-of-the-art screening room, his sound designer, wanting to demonstrate an effect, played a loud, metallic crash in the pitch-dark theatre. Arthur didn't just jump; he cried out and scrambled for the exit, leaving his bewildered team behind. The incident solidified his greatest fear: that he is no longer capable of doing the one thing that has defined his entire adult life. He came to the first session not just to stop being afraid, but with a desperate hope of finding the person he was before the lights went out.
